analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay cash compensation for bumped, delayed, and cancelled flights and to disclose fees, fares, and seat space.
analysis.headline: The Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights was introduced in June 2017 by Senator Blumenthal with three Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, never received a markup or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules airlines must follow when dealing with passengers. It would ban bumping passengers off oversold flights against their will except for safety, require at least $1,350 in cash for anyone denied boarding or seriously delayed, and require automatic ticket refunds and hotel costs for delays within the airline's control. It would also cap fee hikes by requiring fees for bags, seat selection, and changes to be proportional to actual costs, block airlines from further shrinking seat size or legroom, mandate free drinking water and usable lavatories, guarantee passengers' right to sue airlines and bar forced arbitration and class-action waivers in airline contracts, and raise penalties for violating passenger rules while forbidding airlines from negotiating them down.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers: anyone bumped from an oversold flight would get at least $1,350 in cash instead of the current capped amounts; passengers on flights delayed over an hour would get automatic refunds and rebooking; those delayed over four hours would also get $1,350, a meal, and hotel costs for overnight delays. Flyers would see full fare, tax, and fee disclosure before buying, refunds for damaged bags, and protection of frequent flyer miles from unilateral cuts. Passengers would gain the right to sue airlines in court and to join class actions, since forced-arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in airline contracts would be invalid. Disabled passengers would gain a right to sue for discrimination with attorney's fees, and travelers with disabilities would be guaranteed accessible lavatories.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers, especially delayed, bumped, and disabled flyers

how_it_helps.text: Passengers involuntarily denied boarding would receive at least $1,350 per flight in cash, and the current dollar caps on such compensation would be eliminated [S3].

If a flight is delayed or cancelled for reasons within the airline's control, the airline must automatically refund the ticket, rebook the passenger at no extra cost on another carrier if needed, pay $1,350 cash plus a meal for delays over four hours, and pay hotel costs for overnight delays [S3].
Airlines could not charge fees for bags, seat selection, or changes that are unreasonable or disproportionate to their actual costs [S3].

The FAA would prohibit any further reductions in seat size, width, pitch, legroom, or aisle width pending minimum space standards, and airlines would have to publish the space available on each aircraft [S3].

Airlines could not enforce pre-dispute arbitration clauses or class-action waivers in ticket, reward program, or credit-product contracts, and passengers would gain a private right of action against unfair or deceptive practices, including for disability discrimination [S3].
Civil penalties for passenger protection violations would no longer be capped at the standard maximum, and airlines could not negotiate reductions of those penalties with the FAA [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The major airlines, which would bear new mandatory cash payouts for bumps and controllable delays and cancellations, pressure to lower bag, change, and seat-selection fees, the cost of maintaining or expanding seat space and amenities, litigation exposure from a new private right of action and invalidation of arbitration clauses, and larger, non-negotiable penalties for violations. Some of these costs would likely be passed to consumers through fares, though the bill argues fees are currently above cost.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory $1,350 cash payments for delays over four hours and unlimited payouts for voluntary bumping could raise ticket prices and make airlines more cautious about scheduling, which could reduce service to smaller communities — a tradeoff the bill itself acknowledges by directing a study of how weather-related disruptions affect small airports [S3].

A strict seat-size freeze before regulators set new standards could create implementation conflicts for airlines mid-fleet-upgrade, and requiring fees to be proportional to costs is a form of rate regulation that is difficult to administer and audit [S3].

Critics of similar proposals note that requiring interline rebooking on competitors and automatic refunds regardless of notice time can strand passengers rather than help them; the bill relies on DOT regulations and studies to work out many details, adding uncertainty about how protections would actually operate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For travelers, the upside is concrete and large: real cash compensation when an airline ruins a trip, refunds by default instead of by fight, full fee disclosure, and the ability to sue. The main honest cost is that some of it shows up in airfares, and parts of the bill (fee-to-cost standards, interline rebooking) are complex to administer. On balance the bill was designed to shift leverage and money from airline balance sheets to passengers; the serious design questions are about execution, not direction.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, so it never reached the Senate floor, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on June 22, 2017, joined by Senator Markey, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S3][S5].
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the referral — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major airlines came out ahead: they kept uncapped bag, change, and seat-selection fee revenue, capped compensation for bumped and delayed passengers, the freedom to keep shrinking seat pitch, and enforceable arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in their contracts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major airlines and their fee and arbitration practices

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights and sought floor consideration for it.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only named co-introducer.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate majority in the 115th Congress (52 Republicans)
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to sit without floor time; as the chamber's majority it controlled the calendar and took no action to bring passenger-protection legislation to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters in the record (the sponsor and three cosponsors) were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-controlled Commerce Committee took no action; the split followed party lines.

industries.note: The bill targets the industry's core revenue practices: mandatory $1,350 cash payouts for bumps and controllable delays and cancellations, fee caps tied to actual cost, a ban on shrinking seat space, invalidation of arbitration and class-action waivers, and larger non-negotiable penalties. Every major provision takes money or legal leverage away from carriers and gives it to passengers.

industries.industry: Airline frequent flyer programs and airline-branded credit products
industries.note: The bill makes materially changing program terms without reasonable notice or cutting earned benefits an unfair practice, requires standardized disclosure of how miles are earned and redeemed, and voids arbitration and class-action waivers in reward and credit-product contracts. These programs are a major profit center for airlines and their card partners.

industries.industry: Mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver defenders (consumer-facing firms relying on forced arbitration)
industries.note: By voiding pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waiver clauses in airline ticket, reward, and credit contracts and adding private rights of action with attorney's fees, the bill would set a precedent consumer firms have fought in Congress for decades: restoring court access and class actions for ordinary customers.

industries.industry: Online travel agents and metasearch engines
industries.note: Airlines would be barred from withholding schedule, fare, fee, and tax information from online travel agents and metasearch tools and from blocking purchase through them, strengthening sites like these that let travelers comparison-shop across carriers.
